images.note: Script beats: Lincoln's Aug 1862 Greeley letter ('My paramount object... is to save the Union'), the draft proclamation in his desk drawer summer 1862, and the preliminary proclamation after Antietam. Contemporary wartime portrait: albumen silver print by Anthony Berger (Brady & Co.), February 9, 1864. Met object 285876. No second-institution image verifiable from this VM (LOC/NARA/SI blocked; see report).
images.title: Abraham Lincoln (wartime portrait, February 1864)

images.note: Script beats: 1861 war aim ('save the Union'); First Inaugural quote ('I have no purpose... to interfere with the institution of slavery'); the exam's '1861 Lincoln vs 1863 Lincoln' contrast. Pre-war campaign-era portrait: salted paper print by William Marsh, May 20, 1860. Contemporary with the 1861-Lincoln beat. Met object 283191. No second-institution image verifiable from this VM.
images.title: Abraham Lincoln (campaign-era portrait, May 1860)

images.note: Script beat: Frederick Douglass's July 6, 1863 speech ('Once let the black man get upon his person the brass letters U.S....'). Daguerreotype by unknown artist, ca. 1855 — a PRE-WAR likeness, not from 1863; honest date. Met object 282066. No second-institution image verifiable from this VM. [dupe-fix: replaced shared URL]
images.title: Frederick Douglass (daguerreotype, ca. 1855)

images.note: Script beats: Butler's 1861 contraband ruling (three enslaved people at a Union camp in Virginia; 'contraband' = seizable wartime property) and the ~400,000 escapes to Union lines. Contemporary 1861 albumen print by Henry P. Moore. Honest geography note: photographed at Port Royal, South Carolina (USS Vermont), not Butler's Virginia camp — same contraband phenomenon. Met object 286558. No second-institution image verifiable from this VM.
images.title: Contrabands Aboard U.S. Ship Vermont, Port Royal, SC (1861)

images.note: Script beats: Antietam, September 17, 1862 ('bloodiest single day of the war... tactically a draw, strategically the Union victory he needed') and the preliminary proclamation five days later. Contemporary 1862 albumen print by Alexander Gardner. Met object 283192. No second-institution image verifiable from this VM.
images.title: Antietam Battlefield (Alexander Gardner, 1862)

images.note: Script beats: Northern reception of the Proclamation (abolitionist grumbling, Democratic gains fall 1862) and 'why it mattered anyway'. Contemporary wood engraving by Thomas Nast from Harper's Weekly, January 24, 1863 — Northern print culture celebrating emancipation. Met object 429270. No second-institution image verifiable from this VM.
images.title: Emancipation of the Negroes - The Past and the Future (Nast, Jan 1863)

images.note: Script beats: 'freedom followed the armies' — the Proclamation taking effect behind advancing Union lines, through Juneteenth (June 19, 1865, Galveston). Contemporary albumen print by Myron H. Kimball, December 1863, of emancipated people brought from Louisiana. Met object 283194. No second-institution image verifiable from this VM.
images.title: Emancipated Slaves Brought from Louisiana (December 1863)

images.note: Script beat: Europe — Britain and France had abolished slavery, so once the war was 'officially against slavery' no European government could side with the Confederacy. Contemporary European coverage: wood engraving by Amand Jacob from the French Le Journal Illustre, July 23-30, 1865. Met object 742408. No second-institution image verifiable from this VM.
images.title: Emancipated Blacks in the United States (Le Journal Illustre, July 1865)

images.note: Script beats: 'what it freed' — the enslaved people the document named; and King Cotton diplomacy (the Southern cotton economy Britain's mills depended on). Contemporary 1862 albumen print by Henry P. Moore of enslaved people going to the field, Hopkinson's Plantation, Edisto Island, SC. Met object 286557. No second-institution image verifiable from this VM.
images.title: Enslaved people going to the field, Edisto Island, SC (1862)
